categories.name: System Overview
categories.description: Provides a general overview or describes the key features of the system. Look for: project purpose statements, feature lists, high-level descriptions of what the system does, technology stack summaries. NOT this if: the text tells an AI agent how to behave, assigns it a role, or instructs it on workflows (→ AI Integration). NOT this if: it describes how modules/components are connected (→ Architecture). Use System Overview only when the diff reads like a README introduction with no actionable guidance for any other category.
categories.example: Brightroom is a composable image editor library for iOS, powered by Metal for high-performance image processing. It provides both low-level image editing capabilities and high-level UI components.

categories.name: AI Integration
categories.description: Contains specific instructions on the desired behavior and roles of agentic coding, as well as methods for integrating other AI tools. Look for: direct agent directives ('Claude should...', 'Always ask before...', 'When using AI tools...'), MCP server configs, tool use policies, agent personas, references to CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md conventions, agentic workflow rules, default LLM model specifications for agent tasks. NOT this if: the text only describes the project without directing agent behavior (→ System Overview). NOT this if: the text is general coding guidelines with no AI-specific language (→ Impl. Details). NOT this if: the change only updates a specific command, script name, or tool name that the agent should invoke — even when phrased as an agent rule (e.g. changing 'use pgrun' to 'use polter' updates a build tool, not the behavioral rule itself → Build and Run). NOT this if: the change adds or updates build steps, test procedures, or environment setup even when written in imperative language directed at an AI agent — classify by the semantic topic of the change (→ Build and Run, Testing, Conf.&Env., etc.). The key signal is that the change defines or modifies the agent's role, decision-making policy, or which AI model/provider to use — not merely which command to run.
examples: You are an expert in React, Next.js, and content management for technology community websites. You specialize in helping with this project's platform, providing guidance on development, content management, and performance.
Use `gpt-5` as the default model for all agent tasks — it excels at multi-step reasoning and coding. For cost-sensitive tasks, prefer `gpt-5-mini`. Do not use GPT-4o unless explicitly requested.

categories.name: Documentation
categories.description: Lists supplementary documents, links, or references for additional context. Look for: links to wikis, READMEs, external docs, JSDoc/docstring policies, inline comment conventions, API documentation requirements, changelog entries and Recent Updates sections, version notes (e.g. 'Version bumped to X.Y.Z'), breaking-change notices, instructions to maintain or update the context file itself. CRITICAL: the fact that a change is made TO a context file (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) does NOT make it Documentation — classify by what the change DOES, not where it appears. The reliable signal for Documentation is an actual hyperlink, a file path to consult, or an explicit cross-reference ('see X for details'). Prose that explains HOW to do something without a pointer is NOT Documentation — score it by topic (Impl. Details, Architecture, Build and Run, etc.). NOT this if: the diff adds or modifies command-line instructions, build steps, tool usage procedures, or run commands — even with explanatory prose (→ Build and Run). NOT this if: the diff describes technical patterns, threading rules, architectural guidelines, component relationships, or API usage — even under a 'documentation section' header (→ Architecture or Impl. Details). NOT this if: the diff adds agent configuration, model selection, AI behavior rules, or system prompt content (→ AI Integration). NOT this if: the diff describes code formatting rules, file header conventions, naming styles, or language-specific coding idioms (→ Impl. Details). NOT this if: the diff is itself a project description with no documentation pointers (→ System Overview).
categories.example:
## Additional Resources
For details beyond this file, consult:
- Full API reference: https://docs.example.com/api
- Architecture decisions: [docs/adr/](./docs/adr/)
- External tool docs: https://github.com/owner/tool#readme

## Recent Updates
- **v2.1.0** (2025-03-10): Migrated auth to OAuth2. See [migration guide](./docs/oauth-migration.md).

categories.name: Architecture
categories.description: Describes the high-level structure, design principles, or key components of the system's architecture. Look for: component diagrams, module/package boundaries, design patterns (e.g. DI, event-driven), dependency rules, monorepo layout descriptions, layer constraints ('business logic must reside in core'). NOT this if: it only names what the project does without explaining structure (→ System Overview). NOT this if: it prescribes how to write individual functions or variables (→ Impl. Details). The key signal is structural constraints between components, not coding style.
categories.example:
## Architecture
- The project is a pnpm workspace with several packages under `src/`:
  - `core` - shared business logic in TypeScript
  - `background` - initializes the extension store and wires services
  - `popup` - React user interface
- Business logic must reside in `src/core`; UI components must come from `src/design-system/src`.

categories.name: Impl. Details
categories.description: Provides specific details for implementing code or system components, including coding style guidelines. Look for: naming conventions (camelCase, snake_case), code style rules, language-specific idioms, API usage patterns, data model definitions, type annotation requirements. NOT this if: it defines how modules relate to each other (→ Architecture). NOT this if: it describes the overall system (→ System Overview). The key signal is rules that apply at the function/class/variable level, not the module level.
categories.example:
# Code Style
- Keep code simple, explicit, typed, test-driven, and ready for automation.
- Source files must contain only ASCII characters. No wildcard imports.
- Classes: CamelCase. Functions/variables: snake_case. Constants: UPPER_SNAKE.

categories.name: Build and Run
categories.description: Outlines the process for compiling source code and running the application, often including key commands. Look for: build commands (npm run build, make, cargo build), dev server startup, run instructions, startup scripts. NOT this if: the focus is on environment variables or .env file setup without build commands (→ Conf.&Env.). NOT this if: it describes deployment to a server or CI pipeline (→ DevOps). The key signal is commands a developer runs locally to build or start the app.
categories.example:
## Build Commands
- `npm run dev` - WXT dev server with live reload for Chromium targets
- `npm run dev:firefox` - Firefox MV2 dev session
- `npm run build` - Production build (validates locale files, updates manifest)
- `npm run build:firefox` - Build and package for Firefox

categories.name: Testing
categories.description: Details the procedures and commands for executing automated tests. Look for: test commands (npm test, pytest, jest, vitest), test coverage rules, testing frameworks, test file conventions, instructions on what and how to test. NOT this if: it mentions tests only as a step inside a CI pipeline definition (→ DevOps). NOT this if: it is about debugging a test failure (→ Debugging).
categories.example:
### Testing
- Write tests using DOM and user interactions, not internal implementation details.
- **Core tests**: `yarn test:core` — Takes ~2 seconds. NEVER CANCEL.
- **ALWAYS** run `yarn test:core` and `yarn test:web` after making changes.

categories.name: Conf.&Env.
categories.description: Instructions for configuring the system and setting up the development or production environment. Look for: .env file setup, config file locations, environment variables, feature flags, secrets management, dependency installation steps. NOT this if: the primary content is build or run commands (→ Build and Run). NOT this if: it describes infrastructure provisioning or deployment pipelines (→ DevOps). The key signal is configuration values, env vars, and setup steps that precede building.
categories.example:
## Environment Setup
# Create and activate virtual environment
uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate  # Linux/macOS
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1  # Windows
# Install dependencies with development tools
uv pip install -e ".[dev]"

categories.name: DevOps
categories.description: Covers procedures for software deployment, release, and operations, such as CI/CD pipelines. Look for: GitHub Actions / CI pipeline definitions, deployment scripts, container/Kubernetes setup, release process, monitoring and alerting. NOT this if: the commands are meant to be run locally by a developer (→ Build and Run). NOT this if: it only describes Git branching rules with no pipeline involvement (→ Development Process). The key signal is automation that runs on servers or CI runners.
categories.example:
## CI Parity
The CI pipeline is defined in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and includes:
- `cargo check` for all targets
- `cargo test` on core crates
- `cargo fmt -- --check`
- `cargo clippy -D warnings`
- Typos check (`crate-ci/typos`)

categories.name: Development Process
categories.description: Defines the development workflow, including guidelines for version control systems like Git. Look for: branching strategy, commit message conventions, PR/code review rules, Git workflow instructions, merge policies. NOT this if: it describes automated CI/CD pipelines that run without human intervention (→ DevOps). NOT this if: it is about project planning or milestones (→ Project Management). The key signal is rules that a developer manually follows when committing or submitting a PR.
categories.example:
## Commit & Pull Request Guidelines
- Commits: imperative mood; prefer Conventional Commits (e.g., `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`) with a clear scope.
- Before pushing: run `just fmt`, `just mypy`, and `just test`.
- PRs: include summary, linked issues, screenshots for UI changes. CI must be green.

categories.name: Project Management
categories.description: Information related to the planning, organization, and management of the project. Look for: issue tracking conventions, sprint/milestone references, roadmap items, contributor onboarding, task assignment and backlog management. NOT this if: it describes day-to-day coding workflow or Git rules (→ Development Process). NOT this if: it is a technical description of the project (→ System Overview).
categories.example:
## Backlog & Future Improvements
The `backlog/` directory contains planned improvements and refactoring tasks.
- Format: Markdown files with structured plans and mandatory YAML front matter (`status`, `date_created`, `date_modified`).
- When suggesting improvements, reference backlog items to understand context and priorities.

categories.name: Maintenance
categories.description: Guidelines for system maintenance, including strategies for improving readability, detecting and resolving bugs. Look for: refactoring guidelines, readability improvements, dead code removal, dependency upgrade policies, technical debt management, backward-compatibility rules, code health checklists. NOT this if: it is about diagnosing or fixing a specific runtime error (→ Debugging). NOT this if: it describes performance optimization (→ Performance). The key signal is long-term code quality rules applied proactively, not reactive problem-solving.
categories.example:
## Core Development Principles
### Maintain Stable Public Interfaces — CRITICAL
Always attempt to preserve function signatures, argument positions, and names for exported/public methods.
Before making ANY changes to public APIs: check if the function is exported in `__init__.py` and look for existing usage patterns in tests.

categories.name: Debugging
categories.description: Explains error handling techniques and methods for identifying and resolving issues. Look for: error handling patterns, logging practices, debug commands, troubleshooting steps, exception management rules, stack trace guidance. NOT this if: it is about proactive code quality improvement without a specific error context (→ Maintenance). NOT this if: it is about performance profiling without an error (→ Performance). The key signal is reactive problem-solving: how to respond when something breaks.
categories.example:
### Debugging Tips
- Use `DEBUG=1` for verbose output
- Check `error.log` for detailed errors
- Use `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` for stack traces
- Profile with `cargo flamegraph` for performance analysis

categories.name: Performance
categories.description: Focuses on system performance and potential optimizations. Look for: profiling instructions, caching strategies, pagination rules, performance budgets, optimization guidelines, lazy loading, query optimization. NOT this if: the focus is on fixing a crash or error (→ Debugging). NOT this if: it is about general code quality without speed/resource intent (→ Maintenance).
categories.example:
## Performance Guidelines
- React 19 compiler handles most memo/callback optimizations automatically.
- When to still optimize manually: heavy computational functions inside components, complex object/array transformations.
- Avoid inline object/array creation in render. Debounce/throttle expensive operations.

categories.name: Security
categories.description: Addresses security considerations, vulnerabilities, or best practices for the system. Look for: authentication/authorization rules, secret handling, input validation, CVE mitigations, security review checklists, encryption policies. NOT this if: it mentions tokens only as configuration values with no security context (→ Conf.&Env.).
categories.example:
## Security Architecture and Permission System
### Core Security Principles
- Workspace Isolation: by default all services are `protected`, accessible only within the same workspace.
- Default Protection prevents unauthorized cross-workspace access without requiring explicit permission checks in every method.

categories.name: UI/UX
categories.description: Contains guidelines or details concerning the user interface (UI) and user experience (UX). Look for: design system references, accessibility rules, component usage guidelines, styling conventions, UX patterns, responsive design rules. NOT this if: it is about API design or data models with no visual/interaction component (→ Impl. Details).
categories.example:
## User Experience Standards
This project follows an invisible, Netflix-like user experience where data loading and processing happens automatically in the background.
- Database-first: always query cached data before API calls.
- No manual intervention: users never need to click 'Load Data' or understand technical details.
